head.e: From Middle English efd, had, hafd, heafd, hed, heed, hefet, heid, het, hevd, heved, hevid, hiede, hæfd, hæfedd, from Old English hēafod (“head; top; leader; origin”), from Proto-West Germanic *haubud, from Proto-Germanic *haubudą (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *káput (“head”), from *kap- (“head; bowl, cup”).
head.g: The part of the body of an animal or human which contains the brain, mouth, and main sense organs.

head.e: From Middle English heed, from Old English hēafod- (“main”), from Proto-West Germanic *haubida-, derived from the noun *haubid (“head”).

headband.e: From Middle English *hedband, from Old English hēafodbænd, hēafodbend (“headband”), equivalent to head + band.
headband.g: A strip of fabric worn around the head.

headdress.g: A decorative covering or ornament worn on the head.

headlong.e: From Middle English hedlong, alteration of hedling, heedling, hevedlynge (“headlong”), assimilated to long.
headlong.g: With the head first or down.

heads.g: A shouted warning that something is falling from above, mind your heads; heads-up.

headstone.g: A gravestone, a grave marker: a monument traditionally made of stone placed at the head of a grave.

headwaters.g: The source of a river, the set of streams that feed into the river's beginning.

heady.e: From Middle English hedi, hevedi, equivalent to head + -y.

heal.e: From Middle English helen, from Old English hǣlan (“to heal, cure, save, greet, salute”), from Proto-West Germanic *hailijan, from Proto-Germanic *hailijaną (“to heal, make whole, save”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilos (“healthy, whole”). Derived from the adjective at hand in whole.
heal.g: To make better from a disease, wound, etc.; to revive or cure.

healer.e: From Middle English helere, the agent noun of heal; analysed as heal + -er.
healer.g: One who heals, especially through faith.

healing.e: From Middle English heelyng, equivalent to heal + -ing.

health.e: From Middle English helthe, from Old English hǣlþ, from Proto-West Germanic *hailiþu, from Proto-Germanic *hailiþō, from *hailaz + *-iþō. Analyzable as whole, hale, or heal + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
health.g: The state of being free from physical or psychological disease, illness, or malfunction; wellness.

health.e: From Middle English heleð (“man, hero, fighter”), from Old English hæleþ (“man, hero, fighter”), from Proto-West Germanic *haliþ, from Proto-Germanic *haliþaz (“man, hero”).

heap.e: From Middle English hepe, from Old English hēap, from Proto-West Germanic *haup, from Proto-Germanic *haupaz (compare Dutch hoop, German Low German Hupen, German Haufen), from Proto-Indo-European *koupos (“hill”) (compare Lithuanian kaũpas, Albanian qipi (“stack”), Avestan 𐬐𐬂𐬟𐬀 (kåfa)).
heap.g: A crowd; a throng; a multitude or great number of people.

hear.e: From Middle English har, heoren, her, here, heren, from Old English hēran, hīeran, hīran, hȳran (“to hear”), from Proto-West Germanic *hauʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną (“to hear”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti (“to be sharp-eared”), from *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”) + *h₂ows- (“ear”) + *-yéti (denominative suffix).
hear.g: To perceive sounds through the ear.

hearer.e: From Middle English heerar, herere, hyerere, equivalent to hear + -er.

hearing.e: From Middle English herynge, equivalent to hear + -ing.
hearing.g: Able to hear, as opposed to deaf.

hearken.e: From Middle English herkenen (“to listen (attentively); to pay attention, take heed”), from Old English hercnian, heorcnian, hyrcnian, from *heorcian (“to hark”) infixed with -n-, from Proto-West Germanic *hauʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną (“to hear”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti (“to be sharp-eared, hear well”).
hearken.g: To hear (something) with attention; to have regard to (something).

heart.e: From Middle English harte, heorrte, hert, herte, hierte, hirte, horte, huerte, hurte, from Old English heorte (“heart”), from Proto-West Germanic *hertā, from Proto-Germanic *hertô (“heart”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr (“heart”), from *ḱerd- (“heart”).
heart.g: A muscular organ that pumps blood through the body, traditionally thought to be the seat of emotion.

hearted.e: From Middle English herted, hertid; equivalent to heart + -ed.
hearted.g: Having a specified kind or number of heart.

hearth.e: From Middle English herth, herthe, from Old English heorþ, from Proto-West Germanic *herþ, from Proto-Germanic *herþaz, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kerh₃- (“heat; fire”). The modern spelling is from an Middle English/Early Modern English /hɛːrθ/, from earlier /heːrθ/, levelled from inflected forms with /rð/ where the vowel would have been lengthened.
hearth.g: The place in a home where a fire is or was traditionally kept for home heating and for cooking, usually constituted by at least a hearthston

heartily.e: From Middle English hertely, herteliche, heorteliche, from Old English ġeheortlīċe (“whole-heartedly, vigorously”), equivalent to hearty + -ly.

heartless.e: From Middle English hertles, herteles, from Old English heortlēas (“without courage; listless”), equivalent to heart + -less.
heartless.g: Without feeling, emotion, or concern for others; uncaring; cruel.

hearty.g: Warm and cordial towards another person.

heat.e: Either an alternative spelling of het (“heated”), a continuation of late Middle English heet, het (an analogical simple past of heten (“to heat”) created on the basis of bet, the past tense of beten (“to beat”)), or a later analogical formation from the past forms of beten's modern reflex beat.

heath.e: From Middle English heth, heeth, hethe, from Old English hǣþ (“heath, untilled land, waste; heather”), from Proto-West Germanic *haiþi, from Proto-Germanic *haiþī (“heath, waste, untilled land”), from Proto-Indo-European *kayt- (“forest, wasteland, pasture”).
heath.g: A tract of level uncultivated land with sandy soil and scrubby vegetation; heathland.

heathen.e: From Middle English hethen, from Old English hǣþen, from Proto-West Germanic *haiþin, from Proto-Germanic *haiþīnaz (“heathen, pagan”, adjective), equivalent to heath (“heathland”) + -en.
heathen.g: Not adhering to an Abrahamic religion; pagan.

heave.e: From Middle English heven, hebben, from Old English hebban, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną (“to take up, lift”), from Proto-Indo-European *kapyéti, from the root *kap-.
heave.g: To lift with difficulty; to raise with some effort; to lift (a heavy thing).

heaven.e: From a wide variety of Middle English forms including hevene, heven, hevin, and hewin (“heaven, sky”), from Old English heofon, heofone (“heaven, sky”), from Proto-West Germanic *hebn (“heaven, sky”), of uncertain origin.

heavenly.e: From Middle English hevenely, hevenly, from Old English heofonlīċ (“heavenly, celestial, chaste”), equivalent to heaven + -ly.
heavenly.g: Of or pertaining to Heaven, the eternal celestial abode of God or the gods.

heavily.e: From Middle English hevely, hevyliche, from Old English hefiġlīċe (“heavily; grievously”), equivalent to heavy + -ly.

heaviness.e: From Middle English hevynesse, from Old English hefiġnes (“heaviness”). Equivalent to heavy + -ness.
heaviness.g: The state of being heavy; weight, weightiness, force of impact or gravity.

heavy.e: From Middle English hevy, heviȝ, from Old English hefiġ, hefeġ, hæfiġ (“heavy; important, grave, severe, serious; oppressive, grievous; slow, dull”), from Proto-West Germanic *habīg (“heavy, hefty, weighty”), from Proto-Germanic *habīgaz (“heavy, hefty, weighty”), from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to take, grasp, hold”). Equivalent to heave + -y.

hedge.e: From Middle English hegge, from Old English heċġ, from Proto-West Germanic *haggju, from Proto-Germanic *hagjō, from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰyóm (“enclosure”).
hedge.g: A thicket of bushes or other shrubbery, especially one planted as a fence between two portions of land, or to separate the parts of a garden

hedge.e: From Middle English heggen, from the noun (see above).
hedge.g: To enclose with a hedge or hedges.

heed.e: From Middle English heden, from Old English hēdan (“to heed, take care, observe, attend, guard, take charge, take possession, receive”), from Proto-West Germanic *hōdijan (“to heed, guard”), from Proto-Indo-European *kadʰ- (“to heed, protect”).

heel.e: From Middle English hele, from Old English hēla, from Proto-West Germanic *hą̄hilō, from Proto-Germanic *hanhilaz, diminutive of Proto-Germanic *hanhaz (“heel, hock”), equivalent to hock + -le.
heel.g: The rear part of the foot, where it joins the leg.

heel.e: Probably inferred from hielded, the past tense of hield, from Middle English helden, heelden, from Old English hyldan, hieldan (“to incline”), cognate with Old Norse hella (“to pour out”) (whence Danish hælde (“lean, pour”)).
heel.g: To incline to one side; to tilt.

heifer.e: From Middle English heyfre, hayfre, heyfer, from Old English hēahfore, hēahfru, of disputed origin; see the Old English entry for more discussion.
heifer.g: A young female cow, (particularly) one over one year old but which has not calved.

height.e: From Middle English heighte, heiȝþe, from Old English hēahþu, hēhþo, hīehþu (“height”), Proto-West Germanic *hauhiþu, from Proto-Germanic *hauhiþō (compare *hauhaz). Equivalent to high + -t (abstract nominal suffix). The regular pronunciation is now obsolete /heɪt/ (as with other words in -eight).
height.g: The distance from the base to the top of something.

heighten.e: From Middle English heightenen, hyghtenen, equivalent to height + -en (verbal suffix).
heighten.g: To make high; to raise higher; to elevate.

heinous.e: From Middle English heynous, from Anglo-Norman hainous, heinous (compare French haineux) from Old French haïr, hadir (“to hate”) (compare Old French en-hadir (“to become filled with hate”)), from Frankish *hattjan (“to hate”) (compare Middle English hetien). The fluctuation between pronunciations with /eɪ/ and /iː/ is old.

heir.e: From Middle English heir, from Anglo-Norman eir, heir, from Latin hērēs.
heir.g: Someone who inherits, or is designated to inherit, the property of another.

hell.e: From Middle English hel, hell, helle, hælle, from Old English hel, hell, from Proto-West Germanic *hallju, from Proto-Germanic *haljō (“hell, netherworld”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover”).
hell.g: A place or situation of great suffering in life.
To add luster to; to burnish (silver or gold).

helm.e: From Middle English helm (“helmet; crown of thorns of Jesus; warrior; inn or shop sign”), from Old English helm (“helmet”), from Proto-West Germanic *helm, from Proto-Germanic *helmaz (“protective covering”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelmos, from the root *ḱel- (“to cover”). Italian elmo; Old French helme, modern French heaume.
From Middle English helmen, helmi (“to provide with a helmet; (figuratively) to cover; to protect”), from Old English helmian (“to cover”), ġehelmian (“to cover with a helmet; to crown”).
helm.g: To cover (a head) with a helmet; to provide (someone) with a helmet; to helmet.

helmet.e: From Middle English helmet, helmett, a borrowing from Old French helmet, heaumet, a diminutive of helme (Modern French heaume), equivalent to helm + -et. The Old French is itself of Germanic origin (whence Old English helm). Used in English since the 15th century, it has largely displaced helm as the general word.
helmet.g: A hard, protective head covering, typically part of armour.

help.e: From Middle English help, from Old English help (“help, aid, assistance, relief”), from Proto-Germanic *helpō (“help”), *hilpiz, *hulpiz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp- (“to help”).
help.g: Action given to provide assistance; aid.

help.e: From Middle English helpen, from Old English helpan (“to help, aid, assist, benefit, relieve, cure”), from Proto-West Germanic *helpan, Proto-Germanic *helpaną (“to help”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp- (“to help”).
help.g: To provide assistance to (someone or something).

helper.e: From Middle English helpere, from Old English *helpere, from Proto-West Germanic *helpārī (“helper”), equivalent to help + -er.
helper.g: One who helps; an aide; assistant; auxiliary.

helpful.e: From Middle English helpful; equivalent to help + -ful.

helping.e: From Middle English helpinge, helpynge, helpinde, helponde, helpand, from Old English helpende, present participle of Old English helpan (“to help”), equivalent to help + -ing.

helpless.e: From Middle English helples, from Old English *helplēas (“helpless”) from Proto-Germanic *helpōlausaz, equivalent to help + -less.

helve.e: From Middle English helfe, helve; from Old English hielfe, from Proto-Germanic *halbiją. Probably cognate to English half, although Etymonline claims relation from halter and helm.
helve.g: The handle or haft of a tool or weapon.

hem.e: A sound uttered in imitation of clearing the throat (onomatopoeia)
hem.g: Used to fill in the gap of a pause with a vocalized sound.

hem.e: From Middle English hem, from Old English heom (“them”, dative), originally a dative plural form but in Middle English coming to serve as an accusative plural as well.

hemlock.e: From Middle English hemlok, hemeluc, from Old English hemlīc, hymlīc m and hymlīce f (“hemlock, bryony, convolvulus”), of uncertain origin. speculative etymology Compare Old English hymele (“hop-vine, hops”), Old English humele (“bryony, widerton, hair moss, gold-hair, morning glory”), Danish and Swedish humle (“hops”), Icelandic humall (“hops”).
hemlock.g: Any of the poisonous umbelliferous plants, of the genera

hen.e: From Middle English hen, from Old English henn (“hen”), from Proto-West Germanic *hannju, from Proto-Germanic *hanjō (“hen”), from Proto-Indo-European *kan-, *kana- (“to sing”). Etymology 1, noun sense 7 after cock (“male chicken; man's penis”).
hen.g: A female chicken (Gallus gallus), especially a sexually mature one kept for her eggs.

hen.e: From Middle English henne, heonne, hinne, from earlier henene, heonenen, henen, from Old English heonan, hionan, heonane, heonone (“hence, from here, away, from how”), from Proto-Germanic *hina, *hinanō (“from here”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe-, *ḱey- (“this, here”).

hence.e: A later Middle English spelling, retaining the voiceless -s, of hennes (henne + adverbial genitive ending -s), from Old English heonan (“away", "hence”), from a Proto-West Germanic *hin-, from Proto-Germanic *hiz, and Proto-Germanic *-anē.
hence.g: From here, from this place, away.

henceforth.e: From Middle English hennes forth, hens-forþ, hennes-forþ, from modification of Old English heonan forþ with an adverbial genitive suffix. By surface analysis, hence (“from here”) + forth (“forward”).
henceforth.g: From now on; from this time on.

henceforward.e: From Middle English hennes forward, equivalent to hence + forward.
henceforward.g: from now on; from this time on

henna.e: Borrowed from Arabic حِنَّاء (ḥinnāʔ), the name of the tree used to make the dye, probably from Middle Persian (*hannāy-, “to smear, anoint”).
henna.g: A shrub, Lawsonia inermis, having fragrant reddish flowers.

herald.e: From Latin heraldus, from Middle English herald, herauld, heraud, from Anglo-Norman heraud, from Old French heraut, hiraut (modern French héraut), from Frankish *heriwald, from Proto-Germanic *harjawaldaz, a compound consisting of Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“army”) + *h₂welh₁- (“to be strong”).
herald.g: A messenger, especially one bringing important news.

herb.e: From Middle English herbe, erbe, from Old French erbe (French herbe), from Latin herba. Initial h was restored to the spelling in the 15th century on the basis of Latin, but it remained mute until the 19th century and still is for many speakers.
herb.g: A plant whose stem is not woody and does not persist beyond each growing season.

herd.e: From Middle English herde, heerde, heorde, from Old English hierd, heord (“herd, flock; keeping, care, custody”), from Proto-West Germanic *herdu, from Proto-Germanic *herdō (“herd”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerdʰ- (“file, row, herd”). Non-Germanic cognates include Albanian herdhe (“nest”) and Serbo-Croatian krdo.
herd.g: A number of domestic animals assembled together under the watch or ownership of a keeper.

herd.e: From Middle English herde, from Old English hirde, hierde, from Proto-West Germanic *hirdī, from Proto-Germanic *hirdijaz.
herd.g: Someone who keeps a group of domestic animals.

herdman.e: From Middle English herdeman, from Old English hyrdeman; equivalent to herd + man.
herdman.g: Someone who herds animals; a herdsman.

herdsman.g: A person who tends livestock, especially cows and sheep; especially, the foreman among a group of such farmworkers, usually with more knowle

here.e: From Middle English her, from Old English hēr (“at this place”), from Proto-West Germanic *hēr, from Proto-Germanic *hē₂r, from *hiz + *-r, from Proto-Indo-European *kís, from *ḱe + *ís.
here.g: In, on, or at this place (a place perceived to be close to the speaker); compare there.

hereafter.e: From Old English hēræfter (“in the aftertime; later on”). By surface analysis, here + after.

herein.e: From Middle English here-inne, her-in, her-inne, hier-ine, from Old English hērinne, from Proto-West Germanic *hērinna, from Proto-Germanic *hē₂rinna, equivalent to here + in.
herein.g: In this; within this content, context, or thing.

hereof.e: From Middle English hereof, herof, heroffe, her-of, her of, from Old English hērof. By surface analysis, here + of.

heresy.e: From Middle English heresie (Middle English her(esie) + -esy), from Old French heresie (modern hérésie), from Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis, “choice, system of principles”), from αἱρέομαι (hairéomai, “to take for oneself, to choose”), the middle voice of αἱρέω (hairéō, “to take”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ser-.
heresy.g: A doctrine held by a member of a religion at variance or conflict with established religious beliefs.

heretofore.e: From Middle English heretoforn, equivalent to here (“here”) + toforn (“before”), from Old English tōforan (“before”).
heretofore.g: Before now, until now, up to the present time; from the beginning to this point.

hereunto.g: Unto this; up until now; hereto.

herewith.e: From Middle English herwith or her-with, from late Old English herwiþ. By surface analysis, here + with.
herewith.g: with this; especially, with this letter or communication

heritage.e: From Middle English heritage, from Old French eritage, heritage (modern French héritage), ultimately derived (through suffixation) from Latin hērēs. By surface analysis, herit + -age.
heritage.g: An inheritance; property that may be inherited.

hero.e: From Middle English heroes, from Old French heroes, from Latin hērōs (“hero”), from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs, “demi-god, hero”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to watch over, protect”); if so, related to Latin servo (“protect”).
hero.g: Somebody who possesses great bravery and carries out extraordinary or noble deeds.

heron.e: From Middle English heron, heroun, heiron, from Anglo-Norman heiron, from Medieval Latin hairō, from Frankish and Proto-West Germanic *hraigrō, from Proto-Germanic *haigrô (compare Swedish häger and Danish hejre), dissimilation of *hraigrô (compare Old English hrāgra, Dutch reiger, German Reiher).
heron.g: Any long-legged, long-necked wading bird of the family Ardeidae.

hers.e: From Middle English hires, heres, hers, attested since the 1300s. Equivalent to her + -s (compare -'s).
hers.g: That or those belonging to her; the possessive case of she, used without a following noun.

herself.e: From Middle English. Equivalent to her + -self.
herself.g: Her; the feminine object of a verb or preposition that also appears as the subject.

hesitate.e: Borrowed from Latin haesitātus, perfect passive participle of haesitō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), intensive of haereō (“to hesitate, stick fast; to hang or hold fast”).
hesitate.g: To stop or pause respecting decision or action; to be in suspense or uncertainty as to a determination.

hesitation.e: From Latin haesitātiōnem, accusative singular of haesitātiō (“hesitating, stammering”), from haesitō (“hesitate”).

hew.e: From Middle English hewen, from Old English hēawan, from Proto-West Germanic *hauwan, from Proto-Germanic *hawwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kewh₂- (“to strike, hew, forge”). Sense 3 derives from the phrase hew to the line (literally “cut evenly with an axe or saw”).
hew.g: To chop away at; to whittle down; to mow down.

hewn.g: Made or crafted by cutting, whittling down.

hold.e: From Middle English holden, derived from Old English healdan, derived from Proto-West Germanic *haldan, derived from Proto-Germanic *haldaną (“to tend, herd”), maybe derived from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to drive”).

From Middle English hold, holde, from Old English hold (“gracious, friendly, kind”), from Proto-West Germanic *holþ, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz (“favourable, gracious, loyal”), from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to tend, incline, bend, tip”).
